The '''Rousseeuw Prize for Statistics''' awards innovations in statistical research with impact on society. This biennial prize is awarded in even years, and consists of a medal, a certificate, and a monetary reward of US$1,000,000, similar to the Nobel Prize in other disciplines.<ref name="RPwebsite">{{cite web|title= Rousseeuw Prize (about)|url=https://www.rousseeuwprize.org/about |access-date=February 9, 2023}}</ref> The home institution of the Prize is the [[King Baudouin Foundation]] (KBF) in Belgium, which appoints the international jury and carries out the selection procedure. The award money comes from the Rousseeuw Foundation created by the statistician [[Peter Rousseeuw]].

==History==
The first Rousseeuw Prize was awarded on October 12, 2022, at [[KU Leuven]], presented by King [[Philippe of Belgium]].<ref>{{cite web|title=King Philippe presents Prize of 1 million dollars at KU Leuven (extract from television news, in Dutch) |url=https://www.robtv.be/nieuws/koning-filip-geeft-prijs-in-leuven-ter-waarde-van-1-miljoen-dollar-144664 |access-date=November 3, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The Rousseeuw Prize for Statistics (from the website of the Royal Palace, in Dutch and French) |url=https://www.monarchie.be/nl/agenda/the-rousseeuw-prize-for-statistics |access-date=November 3, 2022}}</ref> The awarded topic was ''Causal Inference with application in Medicine and Public Health'', with laureates [[James Robins]], [[Andrea Rotnitzky]], Thomas Richardson, [[Miguel Hernán]] and Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen.<ref>{{cite web|title=Statistics gets $1 million award (Science News)|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/news-glance-lgbtq-nobel-laureates-statistics-prize-and-return-snail-darter |access-date=November 2, 2022}}</ref><ref name = "AMSTAT1">{{cite web|title=First Rousseeuw Prize Awarded for Work on Causal Inference (AMSTAT News)|date=August 2022 |url=https://magazine.amstat.org/blog/2022/08/01/first-rousseeuw-prize/ |access-date=November 2, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=First Rousseeuw Prize for Statistics awarded for pioneering research on causal inference|url=https://nieuws.kuleuven.be/en/content/2022/first-rousseeuw-prize-for-statistics-awarded-for-pioneering-research-on-causal-inference |access-date=November 2, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Rousseeuw Prize winners announced (in Institute of Mathematical Statistics Bulletin) |url=https://imstat.org/2022/07/18/rousseeuw-prize-winners-announced/ |access-date=November 3, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Rousseeuw Prize for Statistics (from RTBF, the French-language public Belgian Radio) |url=https://rtv.auxipress.be/ExternalVideo/Alert?id=GQjXbJHx0m4%3D&lang=fr |access-date=November 3, 2022}}</ref> 

The second Rousseeuw Prize was awarded on December 3, 2024 for work on ''The False Discovery Rate and Methods to Control It'', with laureates [[Yoav Benjamini]], [[Ruth Heller (statistician)|Ruth Heller]], and [[Daniel Yekutieli]].


The third Rousseeuw Prize was awarded in 2026 to ''The R Project''<ref name="Rpoject">{{cite web 
|url=https://www.r-project.org/ |title=The R Project |access-date=2026-08-29 }}</ref>, see also 
[[R (programming language)]]. Half of the prize 
money goes to the five laureates [[Brian D. Ripley]], [[Martin Maechler]], Kurt Hornik,
[[Peter Dalgaard]], and [[Luke Tierney]]. The second half goes to the other 
members of the ''R Core Team''
<ref name="Introduction">{{cite web 
|url=https://www.r-project.org/contributors.html |title=R Core Team |access-date=2026-08-29 }}</ref>.

Nominations for the prize are submitted to its website<ref name="RPwebsite" /> together with letters of recommendation. The organizers of the prize and its ceremony are [[Mia Hubert]] and Stefan Van Aelst.
